posts.author: RENI99

Hi. Similar properties is a better guide - you should know exactly what’s been sold in your complex and nearby complexes in the last 3 months and know how your property compares. 

Why don’t you know exactly what’s the other property sold for? How does it compare to yours? Was it sold at auction and if so how many bidders. What was it advertised at? 

Why is the agent telling you the reserve? And before it’s even on the market? 

Sorry for all the questions!

From what you have written I think the agent will see this as a quick and easy sale. Perfect client. 

What have similar properties been advertised at and what did they sell for? Track the market for a few months - how many opens have you been to? 

Most sellers start with a lower range to attract interest and try to stretch budgets. But it does depend on the area and typical practice. 

By signing the do not provide offers that means that don’t have to adjust the price range before auction based on offers over the range.

Many agents want to identify the lowest price you will sell for to reduce their effort. The difference in commission is not material to them but it may be for you. 

You should have started with 2-3 proposals from agents. All presenting what they think the price range is with comparable properties included. And suggested sell strategy. Is an auction common at this price point in your area?

threads.title: Be wary of SOLD prices on realestate.com - PropertyChat

posts.author: Jacque
posts.text:
For those of you who follow real estate prices and rely on the SOLD prices as quoted on sites such as domain.com and realestate.com, a word of warning: DON'T!! THEY ARE NOT NECESSARILY ACCURATE.



I come across the occasional anomaly when searching for clients, and yesterday I found one particular large and well known local real estate agent (who shall remain nameless at this stage) who had every property I looked up (addresses provided on realestate.com) as different from the actual sales price on RPData. I actually stopped checking after the 10th property, as there wasn't one that matched!



RPData get their information directly from the Valuer Generals office and generally don't put it onto their database until settlement, so their records are accurate (apart from the occasional typo!). It was disturbing, then, to find that this particular agency had "jacked up" the SOLD prices to make themselves appear better. Very worrying, indeed. One property which was proudly advertised as SOLD on realestate.com was for a whopping $170,000 MORE than what it actually sold for.



Not only are practices like this misleading and deceptive to the general buying public, but also to those purchasers who are considering using agencies such as these to sell. How much easier is it going to be to convince them at a listing presentation, that they're the best agent as, according to the SOLD prices on a major website portal, they're getting better "results" than other agencies?!!!

posts.author: MB18
posts.text:
Emailed newsletter (26/11/25) from Michael Spillane at Innovate8 Property Sales on best time to sell:

There’s a lot of misconceptions and false narratives in real estate sales.

One of the most common beliefs amongst sellers is that the Christmas period is particularly quiet and as such, is not a good time to list and sell your property.

In reality, nothing could be further from the truth!

Over the year of 2024, December was our third largest month for the number of sales that were written and back in 2023, we actually made more sales in December than any other month of that year!

At this time of the year, I have many prospective sellers questioning whether now is a good time to list and sell, instead planning a launch of their property in January.

Having worked in real estate for more than 25 years now, what I’ve noticed at this time of the year is that many sellers have great intentions of listing in early January but in reality, life tends to get in the way with school holidays still upon us.

Home owners will often focus on getting the kids back to school and then turning their attention to preparing their house for sale.

They will often interview several agents, spend time preparing their homes for sale (including finding tradespeople and handymen that are usually over-burdened with work at this time of the year) and then taking photos and finally listing their home.

By the time that all of these things happen, it is usually late January or more likely, February and because this timeline is ‘human nature’, you often see a spike in listings in February.

Now don’t get me wrong – listings are very tight and with the huge number of buyers in the market right now, February 2026 won’t be a bad time to sell by any means but there’s ways you can tilt the odds in your favour of a more favourable selling price. 

My advice is this – if you’re ready to go in December, do so!

Because the majority of sellers believe that buyers are not looking to purchase property in December, many decide that they won’t list and as a result, there’s very few new properties that come to the market.

But in any given year (especially a year like this one where the market is incredibly hot), I’ll promise you that buyers are still very much focussed on the market.

A very common phrase that many of them tell us in December and early January is…”It’s frustrating because there’s hardly any new properties coming to the market right now!”

If you don’t believe me, keep an eye on the real estate portals and you’ll see that once we hit the second week of December, new listings slow down dramatically.

But of course, many people are off work and it’s common that the number of online viewings actually increases over the Christmas period.

You’d be amazed how many viewings (and even enquiries) our listings receive on Christmas Day alone!

Perhaps people laze around on the couch after Christmas lunch and peruse through social media on their I-Phones…

eventually becoming bored and next thing you know, they turn their attention back to realestate.com.au and start to scroll through countless amounts of listings.

Over the years, I’ve learned the hard way – don’t take a long holiday over the Christmas period!

Many years ago, I took a holiday between Christmas and New Year…and spent most of my time talking on the phone and answering email enquiries.

Last year alone, we sold three homes between Christmas and New Year…a week that is supposed to be the quietest of the year!

I realise that this advice sits in direct contrast to what many agents will tell you – again, I hear this every year!

I believe that many agents will tell you this because they want to take a holiday and can’t be bothered working over this time…hoping and expecting that you’ll wait for them until a time that they recommend you to sell…a time that just happens to co-include with the time that they arrive home from their holiday.

If you don’t believe me, make some enquiries on many of the limited homes that are for sale and see how long it takes for the agent to get back to you…or at worst, see how long it is before you can actually visit for an inspection.

One of the properties we sold last year was to a buyer that made enquiries on a few different homes listed with a variety of agents but we’d managed to get them through the home, negotiate an offer and sign a contract before any of the other agents even returned their initial enquiry. 

So my conclusion – just go when you[re ready…even if this is in December as this is a time where you can actually achieve a higher price than other times of the year because there’s simply less competition.

One caveat on this piece of advice is that you want to make sure that you don’t take photos when Christmas decorations are up – this can date the listing online very quickly.

If Christmas is already a little too close for you to list, my next piece of advice is to move as quickly as you can in late December of even early January.

It can be a little like peek hour traffic or leaving a concert – if you manage to beat the majority of people, you’ll reap the benefits but don’t get caught in the pack.

My team and I are only taking days off on Christmas day and Boxing day so we’re around for a chat over the Christmas period if you need us.

posts.author: Gockie
posts.text:
Tough one. If you price too high, or without a price you risk qualified buyers that could well be willing to pay what you expect not coming to your opens. If you price low and you dont get the expected demand then you might have to sell low.

For us we had ours listed as for auction, no price listed at the suggestion of our agent. But we didnt get enough people through the door though early on during the sales campaign. So we cancelled the auction and put a price range on the listing we were happy with. We immediately then got a buyer willing to pay what we were happy with in the middle of that range. (There was also another party willing to buy it from that same weekend but they were not quite at the same offer level). It was also a North Western suburb with very few properties on the market.

Now to contrast, another property was listed in my suburb for auction for the same date as mine but very underquoted price imo (different agent).

Anyway, that vendor had heaps of people going to his opens and he ended up accepting an offer a week before their auction date. It may well have been a very successful auction but we will never know now. I actually think he undersold his home by about 100k though.

So, if you have heaps of demand it can turn into a silent auction but you really need people to see the place first.

Edit: I will add our house was weatherboard on low side of the street and the other a brick on high side of street and they had driveway to rear access to possibly add a granny flat so naturally there's a lot of people who would prefer the other house

posts.author: Anthony Brew
posts.text:
Short term drivers include

• Vacancy rates doping 

• Days on market falling

• Auction clearance rate

<60% = buyers market

60-70 = balanced

70%+ = sellers market

Note that auction clearance rate is useful for NSW/Vic, but some locations avoid auctions especially during corrections (ie Perth), so there was some other stat to use but can't remember.

• Median price rising

• Vendor discount decreasing

This has the discount but does not show the history

5% or under seems ok. 10% or over means low demand

• Total rent increasing

But yield would depend if price increase is outstripping rental increase or not.

Here is a bit of a summary 

locationscore.com.au has some of this information and it is $97 for 3 months which seems super cheap compared to pricefinder and corelogic which are pretty damn expensive but I have used none of those before so it is not a recommendation..

Here are the main websites that I use

www.realestate.com.au/invest

www.realestate.com.au/invest

www.yourinvestmentpropertymag.com.au/top-suburbs/

www.sqmresearch.com.au

www.onthehouse.com.au

www.onthehouse.com.au

www.dsrdata.com.au

If you find any more sources for useful data, I would appreciate it.

Important:

You should note that these are short term drivers. You really need to look at the long term drivers first - in particular, population growth, economy & income growth, infrastructure, etc.

For population/economy information, follow @JL1's posts. They are fantastic.

Oh and for excellent Melbourne-specific economic information watch out for posts by @melbournian.

If I understand correctly:

1. Population growth is first (ie macro drivers)

2. Leading to increased rental demand (vacancy rates down)

3. Leading to increased rent and yield (as rent increase outstrips the low growth)

4. Leading to more sales due to higher ROI (ie yield) attracting investors (DOM down, clearance rates up, discounting down, prices rising)

5. Leading to price increase

6. And when price growth is faster than rent growth, yield starts to come down even though total rent is increasing

Also just throwing this in because @David Shih wrote an excellent post there which you might find useful.
